# The First Prejudice

## Whether God, in this day and age, no longer makes use of immediate revelations toward mankind; or whether that which has occurred until now with the so-called Inspired and the new prophets might not be a work of God?

->§ I.<-

No reasonable and enlightened Christian can easily doubt that the Devil is a sworn enemy of the <term>Evangelical Truth: In this 18th-century German context, "Evangelical" refers specifically to the Lutheran or Protestant faith based on the Gospels.</term>, and that he strives with untiring diligence to undermine it, or even to suppress it entirely. For he is the "ancient serpent who leads the whole world astray" (Revelation 12:9 <note>original: "Apocal. XII, 9."</note>). He provokes men from one sin to another and thereafter makes them hardened through the "deceitfulness of sin" (Hebrews 3:13 <note>original: "Ebr. III, 13."</note>). Like a roaring lion, he stalks about everywhere, [seeking] the sheep

<summary>This page introduces the first "prejudice" or theological question regarding whether modern-day "Inspired" individuals and prophets are truly sent by God or are part of a diabolical deception.</summary>

### §. V.

I must, however, necessarily begin my treatise with the question of whether there are still **immediate divine inspirations and revelations** today? because the second point, concerning the "new prophets" or <term>the Inspired <note>The "Inspirirten" or "Inspired" were a radical Pietist sect, primarily the "French Prophets" (Camisards) who fled to Germany, claiming to speak under the direct physical influence of the Holy Spirit.</note></term>, largely depends upon it. ### §. VI.

We strengthen and prove this opinion of ours with the following reasons: I. ### Whether God Today No Longer

could occasionally go outside of [his established order] and do something extraordinary. If God, from the very beginning of the world until the time of Christ—and during that era again for almost an entire century <note>original: "Seculum"</note>—revealed his will to various people through immediate inspiration, why should he not be able to do so today as well, and actually do it? Should he not provide the same care for his current Church that he allowed to be felt in older times? 

To this I answer: that in the divine economy <term>Oeconomie: In this context, the "economy of God" refers to the way God manages and administers human history and the Church.</term> and stewardship over his house, one must not look so much at what God *can* do, but rather at what he *wills* to do. If God could formerly reveal his will even to an unbelieving heathen, why should he not still be able to do so now for one of his believing children? Indeed, I will say even more: according to his unlimited omnipotence, God could even open the mouth of a donkey and restrain the folly of the false prophet Balaam (2 Peter 2:16); how then should he not be able to equip a rational human being as a teacher in an immediate way? 

However, he does not necessarily do everything that lies within his power. In the Old Testament, he performed many and great miracles; similar things also happened at the beginning of the Christian Church. Since that time, however, it has not been particularly observed that he has performed many of the same; and most of what has been presented as miracles is either the deception of men, or base supersti-

# Immediate Revelation [considered] for Humanity

->§. IX.<-

In consideration of this, the second part of the aforementioned prejudice now falls away entirely and is dismissed—namely, the desire to regard and represent as divine those things which have occurred for some time among the **Inspired** <note>The "Inspired" (*Inspirirten*) refers to the Community of True Inspiration, a radical Pietist movement that claimed God spoke through chosen "instruments" in ecstatic states.</note>. I. One finds among them no true **divine calling** <note>original: *Beruffung*</note>, such as was found among all who were true prophets of the Lord. # The Second Prejudice.

### Arnold’s *History of the Church and Heretics* is an incomparably good book.

-> §. I. <-

It is an uncommonly great—but also by many unrecognized—blessing of God that nowadays such a great multitude of useful books come into the public light and are placed before the eyes of the world for general use. **For the dead are the best counselors**; <note>original Latin: "Mortui enim optimi sunt consiliarii."</note> for the dead make the best advisors, as the wise King Alphonsus <note>Likely referring to Alfonso V of Aragon (1396–1458), known as "the Magnanimous," who was a great patron of learning and was famous for this specific saying about books.</note> once said. ### §. V.

When I acknowledge Mr. Arnold as the author <note>original: *Auctorem*</note> of this work, no one should imagine that I believe everything contained within it came solely from him. On the contrary, I firmly believe that he often served merely as a conduit <note>original: *Canal*; a channel or mouthpiece.</note> through which others—who were perhaps even more ill-disposed toward the **Evangelical Church** <term>Evangelische Kirche: In this context, the Lutheran Church as established by the Reformation.</term> than he himself—sought to pour their deadly poison into people’s minds. No extensive testimonies are needed to prove this; the matter itself is evidence enough that he must have "plowed with someone else's heifer" <note>original: *mit einem fremden Kalbe müsse gepflüget haben*; a biblical idiom from Judges 14:18, meaning to use someone else's information or assistance to achieve a result.</note> here and there. 

Consider only the astonishing erudition <note>original: *Belesenheit*; deep knowledge gained through extensive reading.</note> that shines through the work and the vast array of original documents <note>original: *Uhrkunden* (Urkunden); primary sources or historical records.</note> cited throughout. How could it be possible for a single person—who was constantly burdened with many other tasks and who, moreover, produced a great number of other books—to be capable of gathering so much in such a short time? Every person may believe and hold what they wish regarding this; yet I hope I may be granted the freedom to believe that Mr. Arnold must have been supported by various outside assistance. What does it ultimately matter to know where such help came from, if only the work itself had not become such a frightful monstrosity? <note>original: *Mißgeburth*; literally a "misbirth" or "deformity," used here to describe the book as a corrupted or unnatural creation.</note>

->§. VII.<-

I) This book makes the testimony of all **writers** <note>original: *Scribenten*</note> doubtful and introduces a general <term>historical skepticism <note>original: *Scepticismum Historicum*; the philosophical position of doubting the reliability of historical records and accounts.</note></term>. Their **credibility** is also by no means justly overturned because they frequently differ from one another in the details; otherwise, one would have to reject all secular **historians**, and in such a way, one could have no historical certainty at all. Nevertheless, everything in the **church histories** <note>original: *Kirchen-Historicis*</note> that does not agree with his personal notions is suspicious to Mr. **Arnold**. # The Third Prejudice.

**Without doubt, Jansenius and Quesnel <note>Jansenius (Cornelius Jansen, 1585–1638) and Pasquier Quesnel (1634–1719) were leaders of Jansenism, a Catholic theological movement that emphasized original sin and the necessity of divine grace, which brought them into conflict with the Papacy and the Jesuits.</note> must have a very good doctrine, since they are so violently attacked by the Pope and his followers, while being praised by the Protestants.**

->§. I.<-

To praise and highly value something without understanding is indeed a truly foolish thing. Nevertheless, this happens more often than almost anything else. Among the majority of people, the situation is not as the Savior says: *We speak (and praise) what we know*, John 3:11 <note>original: "Wir reden (und rühmen) das wir wissen." The author adapts the biblical verse to include the act of "praising."</note>, but rather: we praise what we imagine to be praiseworthy. Many only need to hear that there is something good to be found in a matter, and the conclusion is immediately ready: that such a thing is entirely free from all blameworthy defects. What in truth hardly deserves to be called a faint ray of the breaking dawn must immediately be called a bright, clear day. One sees this evidently in those affairs which for some time have occurred in the Netherlands and France with Jansenius and Quesnel and their followers. Since in so many writings and accounts about the Roman

I freely admit that this prejudice does not seem to be extremely dangerous, as it is found especially among people of moderate understanding and those who have a poor knowledge of the matter; consequently, there is all the less reason to fear that it should lead to major consequences. However, since it is salutary to untangle even the simplest folk from their errors, I hope I do no wrong if I devote several pages to a closer examination of this. Before I proceed to the matter itself, however, I must first provide a short historical report of the persons whom this prejudice concerns, as well as the disputes they incited.

->§. III.<-

We have already mentioned above that a very special reverence for Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the North African bishop whose writings on original sin and divine grace became the bedrock of Jansen’s theology.</note> was deeply impressed upon Jansenius’s mind. ->§. IV.<-

However, none among all has caused the Roman See more stinging vexation than the world-renowned Paschasius Quesnel; so much so, that it often appeared he might have provided the occasion—if not for its total overthrow—at least for a great upheaval. He himself frequently sought to reject the accusation of Jansenism; <note>Jansenism was a theological movement within Catholicism that emphasized original sin and the necessity of divine grace, often clashing with Jesuit teachings.</note> but his opponents were not as easily persuaded as he might have wished. And indeed, he aligns quite closely with Jansenius, except that he does not wish to be called his pupil, but rather prefers to be named a follower of Augustine. As he explicitly wrote to Cardinal Noris: he was sworn to Augustinian doctrine, a disciple by the authority of God and Christ, <note>original: "Augustiniani dogmatis juratus, Auctore Deo & Christo Discipulus"</note> n) that is, he knows his teaching on grace and free will is from God and Christ, that it is truly certain, and therefore remains its sworn adherent. This excellent man is said to have been born in Paris on July 14, 1634. o) Due to his fine talents, great diligence, zealous piety, and exceptional erudition, he was early on admitted into the Society of the Priests of the Oratory of Bérulle, <note>The Oratory of Jesus was a prestigious French society of priests focused on spiritual depth and education; they were often seen as rivals to the Jesuits.</note> and earned quite extraordinary high esteem.

# Jansenius and Quesnel

This quality was particularly found in a certain Marquis who, out of disgust for the offensive life at court, intended to spend the remainder of his days in quiet solitude. For this reason, he requested Quesnel to provide him with guidance on how he might read the four <term>Evangelists</term> <note>The authors of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note> with benefit and edification. When Felix Vialard, the Bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne *p)* came to see this work, it pleased him so much that he recommended it for diligent reading to all the pastors and <term>vicars</term> <note>Local representatives of a bishop or parish priests.</note> of his <term>diocese</term> <note>The district under a bishop's jurisdiction.</note> through a circular letter dated November 9, 1671. He wrote that the author must have studied for a long time in the school of the Holy Spirit to have reached such a great understanding of the divine mysteries; he likewise encouraged the creator to continue with a further sequel. After Quesnel had brought the work on the entire New Testament to completion, it was released to the public in the year 1671, though with his name concealed. It was accepted by many with exceptional eagerness, though it was not at all to the taste of the <term>Jesuits</term> <note>Members of the Society of Jesus, who were the primary theological and political rivals of the Jansenists.</note>. ...at the first **creation**, **Adam** received a perfect holiness, righteousness, and wisdom by virtue of the **divine image**, and these were not merely bestowed upon him afterward. Whereas **Molina** <note>Luis de Molina (1535–1600) was a Jesuit theologian who sought to reconcile human free will with God's grace; his views were often opposed by those following a strict Augustinian path</note>, along with other **Catholics**, taught that even in the state of innocence, some evil inclinations were nonetheless found in our first parents; **Jansenius** again demonstrates the opposite from many passages of **Saint Augustine** <note>original Latin: "loc. cit. fol. 33. seqv." referring to the previously cited work by Jansenius, folio 33 and following</note>. In a word: throughout the entire work, genuine grains of gold of the true **Christian doctrine** are scattered here and there; in particular, he insists on a **moral teaching** <term>Sitten-Lehre (Ethics/Moral Theology)</term> that is incomparably better than that of the **Jesuits**. ->§ VII.<-

The New Testament of Father <note>original abbreviation "P." for "Pater" (Father)</note> Quesnel, though rejected and condemned by the Pope, nonetheless appears to be filled with an even greater knowledge of the truth. In particular, the moral teaching <term>Morale (Ethics/Moral Theology)</term> which he emphasizes throughout is, in many respects, quite beautiful and remarkable, especially as it is presented in a lively, moving, and pleasant writing style. The 101 Propositions, which the Pope had extracted from it and condemned in his famous Bull <note>The Papal Bull *Unigenitus*, issued by Pope Clement XI in 1713, which targeted Jansenist leanings in Quesnel's work</note>, are renowned not only among Quesnel’s friends but also among many Protestants for being entirely consistent with the Holy Scriptures and the sayings of the Church Fathers <note>original: "Altväter"</note>. It is not necessary to demonstrate this through many examples, as entire writings on the subject are plainly available to the public.

## The Fourth Prejudice.

### One can indeed have more than one wife, or at least one can keep a concubine alongside one's regular spouse.

->§. I.<-

It is no small sign of the great corruption of human nature that man—in those things which God has granted him in a certain measure as a rational creature—seldom knows how to find the proper middle path that is pleasing to God. Instead, he commonly exceeds the boundaries so carefully set by the wise Creator in an unseemly manner. I also concede that the authorities <note>original: "Obrigkeit"</note> for certain reasons, may forbid public and generally practiced polygamy or concubinage; for many a man is hardly capable of providing for his single wife and the children he has fathered with her. What a burden society <note>original: "Societät"</note> would face if he were to take even more wives and only trouble the community with a great multitude of children whom he himself cannot support, and who consequently would disturb and burden others with begging? Did not **GOD** himself say: *Be fruitful and multiply*, Genesis 1:28 <note>original: "Genes. II, 28"; the text cites chapter 2, but the command is found in Genesis 1:28</note>. Furthermore, since **GOD** is a wise being and creates nothing without a cause, whereas many a man feels within himself that he has received more strength <note>original: "Kräffte," referring here to reproductive potency or sexual drive</note> for the multiplication of the human race—so much so that he cannot possibly manage with one wife—who would then doubt that **GOD** should not have permitted such a person to use his strengths for the multiplication of the human race, and thereby look after his own health? <note>This reflects an early modern medical belief that the suppression of sexual "strength" or "seed" could lead to physical illness.</note>

...not least <note>The text continues from the previous page, where the author argues that a high reproductive drive is a gift from God.</note> because in such a way, and in no other, can he protect himself against fornication and adultery. Was there even one **Patriarch** <note>The "Patriarchs" refers to the foundational figures of the Israelites in the Bible, such as Abraham and Isaac.</note> in the **Old Testament** after the Great Flood who had no more than one wife?

Who would now want to say that they lived in a state of perpetual **mortal sin** <note>original: "Tod-Sünde"</note>, and yet could have expected to receive divine grace in such a condition?

# On Practicing Polygamy and Concubinage

**Polygamy** <margin>c) They thus commonly define **polygamy** as a union or marriage entered into with many wives at one and the same time, either with or without laws or formal covenants <note>original: "pactis fœderalibus"</note>.</margin> c) denotes such a state where a man has more than one wife in marriage. By **concubinage**, however, we understand in this context that state / where a man, alongside his regular wife / who participates in all the honor, reputation, and property of the man, also binds himself to one or another female person, with whom he intends to father children, yet in such a way that neither this female person is held equal to the regular spouse in dignity and reputation / nor are the children fathered by her treated equally. Some indeed understand by **concubinage** such a cohabitation <note>original: "Beyschlaff"; refers here to sexual relations within a domestic arrangement.</note> where a man mingles with a female person primarily so that he may satisfy his lust, but while he does not prevent the other purpose—namely, the procreation of children—he does not intend it as the main purpose, but only as a secondary one. In this sense, concubinage is not considered by us here. It is also generally rejected by the <term>moralists</term> <note>Scholars or theologians who study ethics and the "moral" application of divine law.</note> as something indecent that runs contrary to the divine purpose: inasmuch as God did not want something / that is the main purpose / to be considered by humans only superficially / and to be achieved only by chance. ### §. XIII.

I intentionally bypass the remaining objections—namely, that the **Church Fathers** <note>original: "Patres"</note>, **Ambrose**, **Jerome**, and **Augustine**, were poor moralists and had argued with very shallow reasons, and likewise that **Emperor Leo’s** <note>Leo VI the Wise (reigned 886–912), a Byzantine Emperor known for his legal reforms, including those on marriage.</note> edict was not brought forth with any weak cause. For what does it matter? If the matter itself has its own certain foundation, it does not harm it if it is defended by some with poor reasons. What has been cited from the **Papal Decrees** <note>original: "Päbstlichen Decretis"</note> also does not require us to dwell on it at length. ### §. XIV.

To be sure, some still object: **God** indeed had the Prophet **Nathan** expressly remind **David** of, and cite as a great benefit originating from Him, the following: *I have given you,* it says, *the house of your lord, King Saul, and moreover his wives into your bosom,* 2 Samuel 12:8. ### On Polygamy and Keeping Concubines

->§. XV.<-

Therefore, the opponents know of no sound reason to support **polygamy** <note>The practice of having more than one wife at the same time.</note> and **concubinage** <note>A legal or social status where a man lives with a woman as a secondary wife or partner without being fully married.</note>. And certainly, such concubinage is a matter which—even if it were not forbidden in the Holy Scriptures with clear and express words—nevertheless runs contrary to sound reason and natural decency. It would also open the door and gate to the greatest disorders, as a wise man says. 

**Polygamy** is also not to be desired, and it would afford a man little pleasure. I fear many would fare in this matter like that son who said to his father: "If I were not allowed to take two wives, I would not marry at all." When the father then advised him to try it with just one, he immediately found so much annoyance, grief, and misery with this single wife that he said he would gladly not think of the other wife, because he already had to endure enough from this one.

### Man still possesses great and extraordinary powers of the soul in his natural state.

->§. I.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>This preconceived opinion is certainly found among far more people than one might hardly suspect. If they are entangled in all kinds of adversities, they believe they can most easily be freed from them if they consult their own understanding, and they think no further of divine help or assistance. If they wish to undertake something important, how little they care to become partakers of a heavenly blessing for it; how much, on the contrary, do they trust and build upon their own strength, art, and skill? If all sorts of sorrowful and adverse events befall them, their mere reason must serve as a source of comfort; they gather together all the reasons through which they hope to obtain relief for their pain, and they hold the opinion that if one only follows the rules of one's reason in a fitting manner, no misery is so intense and great that one cannot show a candid serenity <term>serenity (Gelassenheit): a key theological concept describing a state of calm, detached acceptance and yielding to God's will</term>.

In spiritual matters, things proceed in much the same way. Many read the most holy Word of God without any illumination requested from on high for that purpose; and yet they hope to accurately grasp its correct meaning. Many go to church without the slightest preparation; and yet they imagine they are hearing, understanding, and applying the divine word beneficially. # The Sixth Prejudice.

### Sunday was not instituted by God, and Christians are not necessarily bound to Sunday.

->Section I.<-

As highly as the benefit of God is esteemed by upright Christians—in that the holy Sunday is given to them as a day of rest for their souls and for their spiritual edification—so basely is this day despised by the children of the world <note>original: "Weltkindern," a term used in Pietist literature to describe people focused on secular pleasures rather than spiritual life</note>. These individuals are accustomed to say here, just as those scoffers of old in the Old Testament used to say regarding the feast days: **"Why must one day be holier than another? When the sun makes every day of the year the same?"** <note>original: "Warum muß ein Tag heiliger seyn / denn der ander? So doch die Sonne zugleich alle Tage im Jahr macht?"</note> Sirach 33:7. <note>The Book of Sirach, also known as Ecclesiasticus, is part of the biblical Apocrypha.</note> No day in the entire week is spent by people with more extravagance <note>original: "Uppigkeit," implying luxury, indulgence, or wasteful behavior</note> than this day, which God has made so uniquely renowned. Should one ask a child of the world what Sunday is, one could take no description other than this from their entire conduct: Sunday is a day on which one can indulge in one pleasurable desire after another, go into the taverns, and there dance, leap, drink to excess, and gluttonize. They suggest that this is sufficient, that one has thereby given Sunday its due, and that the remaining time of the day no longer belongs to God, but to man.

# Sunday is not from God
<meta>catchword: would-</meta>

Therefore, God intended for the Sabbath to be held as holy because He Himself had sanctified it through His own rest from the works of creation. Now, however, this is a universal reason that concerns all of humanity. For all people are to behold and honor God as the Creator of Heaven and Earth; therefore, all people are also obligated to celebrate the seventh day, because God desires the works of creation to be contemplated on that day. 

And in this manner, the **Fathers of the early Church**—whose writings the learned **Mr. Brunsmann** <note>Johann Brunsmann (1637–1707) was a Danish theologian and author who wrote extensively on the Sabbath and against the perceived decay of religious observance.</note> has collected with great diligence—have explained this clear passage throughout the ages. Indeed, we see in this way that the Sabbath was instituted at the very beginning of creation, in that the Lord blessed and sanctified this day because He rested upon it. 

It is also quite certain that neither **Christ** nor the **Apostles** in the **New Testament** abolished the connection to the original Sabbath of creation. For in the entire history of the Gospels and in all the Epistles of the Holy Apostles, not a single passage can be pointed out in which Christians are granted any **license** or **freedom** in this matter. And as for what some might bring forward as a pretext <note>The catchword "wer-" indicates the next page likely begins with "werden," meaning "would be" in this context.</note>

### §. X.

It is further argued that worship in the New Testament is not bound to any specific time or place, but must instead be performed by Christians at all times. However, we have already answered this above by reminding the reader that while a Christian can certainly praise God at all times, it is nevertheless well done for him to also offer his due **sacrifice of praise** to God on certain days specifically. For example, on his birthday, when he must join with David in singing: **I thank thee because I am wonderfully made! Wonderful are all thy works, and that my soul knows right well, Psalm 139:14.** Or on the day of his baptism, when he remembers how he has put on Christ in his holy baptism, Galatians 3:27. A respectable person keeps himself clean every day, yet that does not prevent him from bathing and anointing himself at a certain time. The Sabbath is the day on which upright Christians anoint themselves in a spiritual manner and present themselves to their God as spiritual priests and kings for his service, seeking the oil of joy of the Holy Spirit in the Word and in the Sacraments. If one wishes to appeal to the example of Christ—noting that he did not bind himself so strictly to the Sabbath, Matthew 12:1–8—then everyone knows that Christ, the Lord of the Sabbath, only abolished the Jewish Sabbath <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "ben" suggests the original German word was "aufgehoben," meaning abolished or set aside.</note>

<summary>The author argues that while Christians should worship God daily, setting aside specific days like the Sabbath for spiritual "anointing" is as practical and necessary as regular bathing is for physical cleanliness. He maintains that Christ’s actions in the Gospels only abolished the specific Jewish ceremonial Sabbath, not the concept of a holy day of rest.</summary>

### §. XIV.

# Simple Faith
### 294

Nevertheless, there must absolutely be no lack of a correct knowledge of the main and **fundamental doctrines**—namely, that Christ is their **Redeemer**, and that through Him alone they have access to God’s grace, and must place all their comfort in Him, and must seek **righteousness and salvation** <note>The German *Seligkeit* refers to the state of being saved or eternal blessedness.</note> nowhere else. However, the foundation is the very first and most necessary piece, without which the house cannot stand at all. So it is also with faith. It is impossible for it to exist without the knowledge of fundamental doctrines, although it should afterwards be built up ever better.

### Dippel, or the so-called Christianus Democritus <note>The pseudonym of Johann Konrad Dippel (1673–1734), a radical German theologian, physician, and alchemist who was often in conflict with established church authorities.</note>, has uprightly written and defended the truth.

# Dippel has [upheld] the truth uprightly <note>The header is partially abbreviated; it likely refers to Dippel's own claims of defending the truth.</note>

Because **Theology** had gone so poorly for him up to this point, he felt he must apply himself to something else. Following the manner of most ruined deceivers, he chose **alchemy** <note>original: *Goldmacherey*; the practice of attempting to turn base metals into gold</note>. # The Tenth Prejudice.

## The Jews can likewise be saved in their religion.

->§. I.<-

It is not only in accordance with the rules of sound reason, but also according to true Christianity, that one seeks—as far as possible—to abstain from the company of those who bear a general hatred toward other people who are not of their kind, but especially toward Christians. Such people manifest this enmity through the blasphemy and disparagement of the Christian religion, as well as through actual harmful deeds, through fraud, and through injustice in trade and commerce. According to the rules of reason and the <term>Law of Nature</term> <note>The "Law of Nature" (Lex Naturalis) refers to a system of ethics that 18th-century thinkers believed was inherent to human reason and applicable to all people regardless of their specific faith.</note>, a human being is bound to tolerate the other alongside him as long as he keeps the peace, and to show him the duties of universal love. As soon as the other no longer behaves as a peaceful member of society, but breaks the duties of <term>sociality</term> <note>Sociality (Socialität) was a central concept in Enlightenment political philosophy, referring to the natural inclination and duty of humans to live together in a peaceful, organized society.</note> in all sorts of ways, then the other party is authorized, depending on the circumstances, to restrain him even with force. Nor are they all children because they are Abraham’s seed; but "In Isaac shall your seed be called."** That is: those who are children according to the flesh are not the children of God; rather, the children of the promise are counted as the seed (Romans 9:6–9). 

Paul intends to say this: if God has promised that He would establish an eternal covenant with the seed of Abraham and with the people of Israel, then you must know above all else who is meant by the "seed of Abraham" and the "people of Israel." Namely, the Spirit of God does not mean all those who descend from Abraham by natural birth, but rather those who are Abraham’s children according to faith, and who have been born again through the word of promise—that is, through the Gospel—whether they be Jews or Gentiles. Thus, the "people of Israel" also does not signify the twelve tribes

## II. Index.
->catchword: Errata<-

**Prophetesses**, pagan ones, had movements of the body 28 <note>This likely refers to the ecstatic or convulsive physical states reported of ancient oracles, such as the Pythia at Delphi, which Christian authors often contrasted with the calm of biblical prophets.</note>
**Water**, a proverb concerning it 447
**Women** are praised 310; are suited for study 311; what the cause may be that not many become learned <note>original: "ibid." [ibidem, in the same place]</note> 311.
**Wisdom**, true wisdom, in what it consists 365
**Worldly Wisdom** [Philosophy], its great usefulness 329 <note>In this period, "Welt-Weißheit" (Worldly Wisdom) was the standard term for secular philosophy as opposed to theology.</note>
**Rebirth** [Regeneration] occurs through the Divine Word 352
**Will of man** is by nature entirely weakened 212 <note>A reference to the doctrine of "total depravity" or the corruption of the human will following the Fall of Man.</note>
**Word of God** is often read without asking for enlightenment 186; is recorded simply and clearly 276
**Miracles**, the new ones are a fraud 20 <note>The author likely refers to contemporary claims of miracles by rival religious sects or "wonder-workers," which he views with skepticism.</note>

# Z.

**Drawing**, the art of, whether it is blameworthy 326
**Fabric** [Cloth] should have simple weave 283 <note>Likely a reference to religious or moral arguments for modesty and plainness in dress, common in Pietist or similar reformist literature.</note>

<meta>This page contains the "Errata," a standard list of corrections for typographical and linguistic errors found throughout the book. It appears after the index to ensure that the reader can rectify mistakes in the theological and historical text, maintaining the scholarly integrity of the work.</meta>

## Errata.

Page 6, line 28: instead of Marians, **Marinos** <note>Marinos of Neapolis was a Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer.</note>. p. 21, l. 4: instead of *könnet* [you can], **könnte** [could]. p. 28, l. 1: instead of **similar** <note>original: "παραπλήσιον" [paraplēsion]</note>, **similar** <note>original: "παραπλήσιον"; this entry likely corrects a subtle printing error in the Greek diacritics or typeface that the OCR presents as identical.</note>. p. 29, l. 10: instead of *the year 1707*, **the 1707th year**. p. 31, l. 11: instead of *one*, **this**. p. 33, l. 2: instead of *spargitet*, **spargiret** <note>A correction to the Germanized form of the Latin 'spargere,' meaning to scatter or sprinkle.</note>. p. 83, l. 12: instead of **Doctor**, **Doctor**. l. 22, 23: instead of **Jansenius**, **Jansenius** <note>Cornelius Jansenius was a Dutch theologian whose teachings led to the Jansenist movement; the correction likely pertains to the specific font used for his name.</note>. page 171, penultimate line: instead of Salem, **Salen**. p. 183, l. 13: instead of *corqus*, **body** <note>original: "corpus"</note>. l. 14: instead of *habentur*, **let it be held** <note>original: "habeatur"</note>. p. 193, l. 12: instead of **helps** <note>original: "adjuvat"</note>, **helps** <note>original: "adjuvat"</note>. p. 196, l. 23: instead of *infectum* [unfinished], **introduced** <note>original: "invectum"</note>. p. 222, l. 6: **It** / **So**. p. 226, l. 27: instead of *eingesetzet*, **eingesetzt** <note>A minor spelling correction of the word for 'inserted' or 'appointed'.</note>. p. 250, l. 4: in the citation, instead of *most talkative* <note>original: "locutissimus"</note>, read **most acute** <note>original: "Acutissimus"; this is a significant correction from a critique of someone's wordiness to a praise of their sharp intellect.</note>. p. 262, l. 1: it stands **of the dead** <note>original: "νεκρῶν" [nekrōn]</note>, it should stand so: **of the dead** <note>original: "νεκρῶν"</note>. p. 272, l. 1: instead of Quenstads, **Quenstedts**, instead of Osiannri, **Osiandri** <note>These corrections fix the names of prominent Lutheran theologians Johannes Andreas Quenstedt and Lucas Osiander.</note>. p. 278, l. 20: instead of *Christi*, **Christ** <note>original: "Christe"; changing the Latin case from the genitive 'of Christ' to the vocative 'O Christ'.</note>. p. 286, in the Observations, l. 4: instead of *aequiescit*, **acquiesces** <note>original: "acquiescit"</note>. p. 314, l. 10: instead of *usual* <note>original: "solito"</note>, **solid** <note>original: "solido"</note>. p. 320, l. 16: instead of **brain** [Gehirn], **in secret** [in geheim]. p. 321, last line: instead of *agnoscendis*, **of the one recognizing** <note>original: "agnoscentis"</note>. p. 341, last line: instead of *unterdrucken*, **oppress** <note>original: "unterdrücken"; a correction of a missing umlaut which changes the vowel sound and meaning.</note>. p. 342, section 2, l. 1: instead of **clear**, **clear**. p. 353, l. 4: instead of **and** [und], **from** [von]. p. 366, l. 22: instead of *spiritaliter*, **spiritually** <note>original: "spiritualiter"</note>.
